articles.title: How Does a Touch Screen Work?
articles.dek: You touch your phone every day. But how does it know where your finger is?

sources.name: ScienceAlert: How does a touchscreen actually work?
Embedded Computing Design: The Royal Air Force and the invention of the modern touchscreen

paras: Have you ever used a touch screen? Of course you have! Phones, tablets and even some classroom boards have got one. You touch the glass, and the screen answers. But how does it know where your finger is? Let's find out step by step.
First, look at the screen of a phone. Under the glass, there is a very thin layer. You can't see it, but it carries a little electricity. It works like a net of tiny lines across the whole screen.

Your body can carry electricity too, because it has a lot of water and salt inside. When your finger touches the glass, the electricity in the layer changes a little at that place. Don't worry. It is much too small to feel. A tiny computer chip in the phone notices the change. Then it finds the exact place of your finger in less than a second.

Have you ever tried to use your phone with winter gloves on? It doesn't work, does it? Cloth can't carry electricity, so the screen doesn't notice your finger. Some gloves have special thread in the fingertips. This thread can carry electricity. With these gloves, you can send messages in the snow!

A phone screen doesn't need a hard push. A soft touch is enough. That is why a wooden pencil doesn't work on it. But some older screens, like the ones on ticket machines, were different. You had to press them hard with your finger.

Touch screens are not new. Eric Johnson, a British engineer, made one of the first finger touch screens in 1965. He wanted to help people who control planes in the sky. For many years after that, most families didn't have computers at home.

Today, many children have never used a phone with buttons! But a lot of grandparents have never had a phone with a screen like yours. Ask your grandma or grandpa: "Have you ever used a touch screen?" Maybe you can show them how it works.

articles.title: The Night Before Our Holiday
articles.dek: Sofia's family is flying tomorrow. Is everyone ready? Not yet!
paras: Hi everyone! It's Sofia again. Tomorrow my family is flying to Lisbon to visit my grandma for a week. It's ten o'clock at night, and our house is a mess. Here is a list of what we've done and what we haven't done yet.

Mum has already packed her suitcase. She always plans everything early. Dad hasn't started yet. He says he only needs ten minutes. My little brother Tom has just put his football in his bag. He hasn't packed any clothes yet, but he's got three toys and a torch!

What about me? I've already chosen my clothes. I've packed four T-shirts, my swimsuit and a warm jumper for the evenings. Grandma's house is near the sea, so I want to swim every day. But I haven't found my sunglasses yet. I think Tom has taken them again!

We've also had a small problem. Our cat, Pepper, can't come with us. Our neighbour, Mrs Rossi, is going to feed her. I've just written a note for her with all the information. Pepper eats twice a day, and she loves fish.
Have we printed the plane tickets yet? No, we haven't, because they're on Dad's phone. Have we got our passports? Yes! Mum has already put them in her handbag. She checked them three times!

Update, half past eleven: Dad has just finished his packing. It took him an hour, not ten minutes! And guess what? Tom has just found my sunglasses under his bed. He says he didn't take them. Now everything is ready.

Our taxi is coming at five o'clock in the morning, so I'm going to bed now. Do you know any fun places in Lisbon? Write your tips in the comments below! My next post comes from Grandma's kitchen. Bye!

articles.title: Fifty Years on Hill Street
articles.dek: Mr Mensah has lived in the same house for fifty years. What has he seen?
paras: Every month, our school magazine talks to someone from our town. This month, Nina Park from Year 9 visited Mr Kwame Mensah. He is seventy-eight years old, and he has lived on Hill Street for fifty years.

Nina: How long have you lived here, Mr Mensah? Kwame: I've lived in this house since 1975. I came here from Ghana when I was twenty-seven. At first, I didn't know anyone. But the neighbours were kind, and they soon became my friends.

Nina: How has the street changed? Kwame: Oh, a lot! In 1975, there was a small shop on the corner. It sold bread, milk and sweets. It closed in 1998, and now there's a café there. Also, children played in the street every evening. Today they often stay inside with their phones!

Nina: What was your job? Kwame: I was a bus driver for thirty-five years. I drove the number 12 bus every day. I've met hundreds of people from this town on my bus. Some of them still say hello to me in the street.

Nina: Have you got a big family? Kwame: Yes. I married my wife, Grace, in 1980. We've got two daughters and four grandchildren. My youngest grandson goes to your school! He visits me every Sunday, and we play chess. He has never won a game, but he's getting better.

Nina: What is the best thing about living here? Kwame: The people. I've had some hard times, but my neighbours have always helped me. Last winter, I was ill for three weeks. The family next door did my shopping every day. You can't buy that kind of friendship.
Nina: Thank you, Mr Mensah! Kwame: Thank you, Nina. Come back and visit me again. I've got a lot more stories!

When he was ill, the family next door did his shopping.
kps.q: Who did his shopping last winter?

mindmap.question: What has Mr Mensah's life on Hill Street been like?

summary.intro: Choose the three sentences that tell the main ideas of the interview.
summary.model: Mr Mensah has lived on Hill Street since 1975, and the street has changed a lot. He loves living there because his neighbours have always helped him.

options.t: Mr Mensah has lived on Hill Street for fifty years.
options.why: This is who the interview is about.
options.evidence: He is seventy-eight years old, and he has lived on Hill Street for fifty years.

options.t: The street has changed a lot since 1975.
options.why: This is an important part of the interview.

options.t: For him, the best thing about the street is the people.
The old shop sold bread, milk and sweets.
options.why: True, but it is only a small detail.
options.evidence: It sold bread, milk and sweets.

options.t: Mr Mensah wants to move to a new town.
His grandson always wins at chess.
options.why: Wrong: he has never won a game.
options.evidence: He has never won a game, but he's getting better.

speak.p: Tell me about an older person in your family. How long have you known them? What do you do together?
speak.hint: I've known … since … / Last weekend we …

write.p: Write an email to your English teacher about an older person in your town. Write 25 words or more.
steps: Say how long they have lived there.
Say one thing they did in the past.
